items.learning_item: Write unit tests for preprocessing, inference, and utility functions.

voice.prompt:
Draw the line for me between unit tests, integration tests and evaluations in an LLM-backed product.

What can a unit test tell you about that system, what can it never tell you, and how would you allocate a fixed testing budget across the three?
follow_up_probes: Give me one thing you would assert in a unit test about an LLM call.
Your eval score drops two points. Does that block the release?
Where do you put the boundary between a flaky test and a real signal?
expected_answer_outline: Unit tests cover deterministic surface: prompt assembly, schema validation, parsing, retry logic, token budgeting, tool-argument construction — with the model stubbed.
States clearly what unit tests cannot cover: output quality, groundedness, refusal behaviour, regression from a model version change.
Integration tests cover wiring: real client against a recorded or sandbox endpoint, timeouts, error mapping, end-to-end contract.
Evals cover quality on a curated set with graded rubrics or an LLM judge, tracked over time with a regression threshold rather than a pass/fail gate.
Allocates budget with reasoning — typically the majority to fast deterministic tests, a thin integration layer, and a small but genuinely curated eval set.
Distinguishes a blocking gate from a monitored signal, and treats eval variance explicitly (repeat runs, confidence in the delta).
voice.sample_strong_answer:
Unit tests own everything deterministic around the model. Prompt assembly given a context object, token budget enforcement, JSON schema validation of the response, what happens on a malformed response, retry and backoff behaviour, tool-argument construction. All of that runs with the client stubbed, in milliseconds, and a failure points at exactly one function. If I can only assert one thing about an LLM call in a unit test, it is that a malformed or truncated response is handled without crashing and without silently returning a partial object.

What a unit test can never tell me is whether the answer was good. It cannot detect that a model version change made the summaries less grounded, or that the system started refusing a legitimate category of request. Those are properties of the model plus the prompt, not of my code.

Integration tests sit in between: real client, recorded or sandbox endpoint, verifying that the wiring, timeouts and error mapping actually hold. Thin layer, because they are slow.

Evals are a different instrument entirely. A curated set with graded rubrics, run on a schedule and before release, tracked as a time series. The key distinction is that a unit test is a gate and an eval is a signal. A two-point drop does not block a release on its own — I would first ask whether it is inside the run-to-run variance, which means I need the eval repeated enough times to know what that variance is. If the drop is real and on a dimension that matters, it blocks; if it is real and on a dimension I do not care about, it goes on the dashboard.

On budget: most of it goes to the fast deterministic layer because that is where the cost per bug caught is lowest. A thin integration layer. And a small eval set that is genuinely curated — fifty carefully chosen cases with real disagreement in them beat five hundred scraped ones, because the scraped set mostly measures things every model already gets right.

evaluation_criteria.criterion: Draws defensible boundaries with concrete examples in each category.
States plainly what unit tests cannot detect in an LLM system.
Distinguishes blocking gates from monitored signals and handles eval variance.
Allocates effort with a stated rationale rather than a generic pyramid.

common_pitfalls: Treating evals as just another test suite with a pass/fail threshold.
Claiming temperature 0 makes LLM output unit-testable for quality.
Reciting the test pyramid with no LLM-specific content.
No acknowledgement of run-to-run variance in eval scores.
red_flags: Would gate every release on an absolute eval score with no variance estimate.
Sees no need for any deterministic tests because 'the model is the product'.

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Draws defensible boundaries with concrete examples in each category.
States plainly what unit tests cannot detect in an LLM system.
Distinguishes blocking gates from monitored signals and handles eval variance.
Allocates effort with a stated rationale rather than a generic pyramid.

items.learning_item: Use Git branches, commits, pull requests, and merge-conflict resolution.

mcq.stem: `checkpoints/model.pt` was committed last week. A teammate now adds `checkpoints/` to `.gitignore`, but the file still shows as modified on every training run. Why?
options: Binary files are exempt from `.gitignore` unless a matching entry exists in `.gitattributes`
`.gitignore` is evaluated at clone time, so existing clones need to be re-cloned
`.gitignore` only applies to untracked files; this file is already in the index
`.gitignore` patterns need a leading slash to match a directory at the repository root
The ignore file must be committed before it takes effect, and the teammate only staged it

distractor_rationale.misconception: Pattern syntax detail that is not the cause here.
Plausible-sounding but false; the working-tree file is read regardless of commit state.
Invents a binary exemption.
Invents clone-time evaluation.

mcq.explanation: `.gitignore` is consulted only when Git decides whether to start tracking an *untracked* path. Once a file is in the index, ignore rules are bypassed entirely. Run `git rm --cached checkpoints/model.pt` and commit that removal.

items.learning_item: Use Git branches, commits, pull requests, and merge-conflict resolution.

mcq.stem: You ran `git commit --amend` on a commit that was already pushed to a shared branch. What is the consequence?
options: The commit gets a new SHA, so the local and remote branches diverge
The remote is updated automatically on the next `git fetch`
The original commit is deleted from the remote and the branch loses one commit
Git creates a merge commit on push to reconcile the two versions
Nothing changes remotely, because `--amend` only edits the local commit message in place

distractor_rationale.misconception: Ignores that amending rewrites the commit object.
`fetch` never writes to the remote.
Confuses the local rewrite with a remote deletion.
Push does not auto-merge.

mcq.explanation: `--amend` replaces the commit with a new object and therefore a new SHA. The remote still has the old one, so the push is rejected as non-fast-forward. Resolving it needs `--force-with-lease` and coordination with anyone who already pulled — which is why amending after pushing to a shared branch is discouraged.

items.learning_item: Manage dependencies using virtual environments and dependency files.

mcq.stem: A teammate generated the project's dependency file with `pip freeze > requirements.txt` inside their active venv. What is the most significant problem with the result?
options: It cannot be consumed by `pip install -r`, which requires a different format
It excludes packages installed with `pip install -e`, so locally developed packages go missing entirely
It sorts alphabetically, which breaks the install order dependencies rely on
It records the whole environment — transitive packages and local editable paths — not the direct requirements
It omits version numbers for transitive packages, so installs are not reproducible across machines

distractor_rationale.misconception: `pip freeze` does pin versions — that part is fine.
The output is directly consumable.
Editable installs appear, just in an unportable form.
Install order is resolved by pip, not by file order.

mcq.explanation: `pip freeze` dumps the environment, not the project. You lose the distinction between what you asked for and what came along, and paths such as `-e /home/alice/pkg` or platform-specific builds make the file unusable elsewhere. Keep hand-written direct dependencies and generate a separate lock file (pip-tools, uv, Poetry) for the full pinned set.

items.learning_item: Work with Linux commands, environment variables, and basic shell scripts.

mcq.stem: `setup.sh` contains `export MODEL_DIR=/data/models`. After running `./setup.sh`, `echo $MODEL_DIR` in the same terminal prints nothing. Why?
options: `export` requires the variable to be declared before it can be exported
The script ran in a child shell, which cannot modify its parent's environment
The variable was set but `echo` needs `${MODEL_DIR}` braces to expand a path containing slashes
`export` only persists for the lifetime of the current command, not the current script
The script needs `chmod +x` before `export` statements take effect

distractor_rationale.misconception: Invents a declaration requirement.
Braces are optional here.
Misstates `export` scope.
Without `chmod +x` the script would not have run at all.

mcq.explanation: `./setup.sh` forks a new shell. Its environment dies with it. `source setup.sh` (or `. setup.sh`) executes the commands in the current shell, so the export persists.

items.learning_item: Use Git branches, commits, pull requests, and merge-conflict resolution.

mcq.stem: What is the difference between `git pull` and `git pull --rebase` on a feature branch that has local commits and whose remote has moved forward?
options: Plain `pull` fetches only; `--rebase` is what actually integrates the changes
`--rebase` is faster but otherwise produces an identical commit graph
Plain `pull` replays your local commits on top of the fetched remote, while `--rebase` records the merge commit
`--rebase` discards the local commits and takes the remote version
Plain `pull` records a merge commit; `--rebase` replays local commits onto the remote, giving new SHAs

distractor_rationale.misconception: Confuses rebase with a hard reset.
Plain `pull` is fetch + merge, so it does integrate.
The graph differs materially.
Straight inversion of the two behaviours.

mcq.explanation: `git pull` = `fetch` + `merge`, which records a merge commit. `git pull --rebase` = `fetch` + `rebase`, which rewrites your local commits onto the new base — linear history, but new SHAs, so it is safe only for commits you have not shared.

items.learning_item: Work with Linux commands, environment variables, and basic shell scripts.

mcq.stem: A `.env` file sits next to `train.py` containing `BATCH_SIZE=64`. `os.environ["BATCH_SIZE"]` raises `KeyError` when the script runs. What is the correct explanation?
options: `.env` files are read automatically only when the file is named `.environment`
Python does not read `.env` files; something else has to load it into the process environment first
`os.environ` only exposes variables exported by the parent shell with `declare -x`
The file needs a `export ` prefix on each line for Python to parse it
`os.environ` caches at interpreter start, so the file must be created before Python launches

distractor_rationale.misconception: Invents a filename convention.
Half-true about export, but the real issue is nothing read the file at all.
The prefix matters for `source`, not for Python.
Caching is real but irrelevant — the value was never in the environment.

mcq.explanation: `.env` is a convention, not a mechanism. Docker Compose, most process managers and the `python-dotenv` library know how to read it; the Python interpreter does not. Either call `load_dotenv()` explicitly or have the runtime inject the variables.

items.learning_item: Use Git branches, commits, pull requests, and merge-conflict resolution.

mcq.stem: During `git merge main` on your feature branch you hit a conflict and run `git checkout --ours config.yaml`. Which version do you get?
options: A file containing both versions with conflict markers preserved
The version with the most recent commit timestamp of the two
The version from `main`, since `--ours` refers to the branch being merged in
Your feature branch's version, because during a merge `--ours` refers to HEAD, the branch you are on
The common ancestor's version, since `--ours` selects the merge base

distractor_rationale.misconception: Describes `--theirs` during a merge.
Confuses `--ours` with the base stage.
That is the default conflicted state, not what `--ours` produces.
Git does not resolve by timestamp.

mcq.explanation: During a merge, `--ours` is HEAD — your current branch — and `--theirs` is the incoming branch. The trap is that these invert during a **rebase**, because rebase replays your commits onto the upstream, making the upstream `--ours` and your own work `--theirs`. Check `git status` before reaching for either.

items.learning_item: Use Git branches, commits, pull requests, and merge-conflict resolution.

mcq.stem: A bad commit reached `main` and three people have already pulled it. Which action is appropriate, and why?
options: `git revert <sha>`, because it adds a new commit undoing the change while leaving shared history intact
`git rebase -i` to drop the commit, then force-push, since interactive rebase is the supported way to remove commits
`git checkout <sha~1> -- .` and commit, because it restores the previous file contents
Delete and recreate `main` from the last good commit so everyone starts clean
`git reset --hard HEAD~1` then force-push, because it removes the bad commit cleanly

distractor_rationale.misconception: Rewrites shared history; the three collaborators get divergent branches on their next pull.
Same problem as A — any history rewrite plus force-push breaks collaborators.
Restores tracked file contents but not deletions, and hides the intent from history.
Maximum disruption for the same effect as a revert.

mcq.explanation: On a branch others have pulled, the rule is: add history, do not rewrite it. `git revert` creates a new commit that inverts the change, so every clone converges on a fast-forward pull. Reset, rebase and branch recreation all require force-pushing and leave collaborators with divergent histories.

items.learning_item: Manage dependencies using virtual environments and dependency files.

mcq.stem: `requirements.txt` pins only direct dependencies (`transformers==4.40.0`, `fastapi==0.110.0`). A build that worked last month now fails in CI with an unrelated import error. What is the most likely cause and the right fix?
options: The Python patch version changed on the CI image; pin the Python version instead
`pip` changed its resolver; pin the pip version in the CI step
Direct pins must use `>=` rather than `==` so pip is free to resolve a compatible set
The venv was cached from an earlier run; clear the CI cache and rebuild from scratch
A transitive dependency shipped an incompatible release; install from a lock file

distractor_rationale.misconception: A cache would preserve the working set, not break it.
Worth pinning, but it does not explain an import error from a package you did not change.
Resolver changes happen but rarely produce this symptom.
Loosening pins makes drift more likely, not less.

mcq.explanation: Pinning only what you named leaves everything underneath floating, so any transitive release can change your environment without any change on your side. The fix is a two-file discipline: human-authored direct requirements, plus a machine-generated lock file with the fully resolved, hash-pinned set that CI and production install from.

items.learning_item: Manage dependencies using virtual environments and dependency files.

mcq.stem: An API key was committed in `.env` three weeks and forty commits ago. `git rm .env` was committed today. What still needs to happen?
options: Squash the last forty commits, which collapses the secret out of the log
Nothing further; the file no longer exists at HEAD
Rotate the key immediately; history rewriting with `git filter-repo` is secondary cleanup
Rewrite history first with `git filter-repo`; rotation is unnecessary once the secret is gone from every commit
Add `.env` to `.gitignore`, which retroactively removes it from history

distractor_rationale.misconception: The secret is still readable in every historical commit.
Inverts the priority — the secret has been exposed for three weeks and may already be cloned or scraped.
`.gitignore` has no retroactive effect.
Squashing merges commits but the blob remains reachable.

mcq.explanation: Once a secret has been pushed, assume it is compromised — forks, clones, CI caches and scrapers all may hold it. Rotation is the only action that actually revokes access, and it is the first thing to do. History rewriting is worthwhile cleanup but it is slow, disruptive and cannot recall what has already been fetched.

items.learning_item: Work with Linux commands, environment variables, and basic shell scripts.

mcq.stem: A CI script begins with `set -e` and contains `python preprocess.py | tee preprocess.log`. `preprocess.py` exits non-zero but the pipeline continues to the training step. Why?
options: A pipeline reports only its last command's status, so `tee` masks the failure
`set -e` must be written as `set -eu` to take effect inside CI runners
`tee` catches the error and rewrites the exit status to 0 by design
Python scripts always exit 0 unless `sys.exit()` is called with an explicit status
`set -e` does not apply to commands whose output is redirected or piped elsewhere

distractor_rationale.misconception: Redirection is not the exempting condition.
`-u` controls unset variables, not this.
`tee` reports its own status; it does not rewrite anything.
An uncaught exception exits non-zero.

mcq.explanation: By default a shell pipeline reports only the last command's status, so `python ... | tee ...` returns `tee`'s zero and `set -e` sees success. The standard prelude is `set -euo pipefail`, which makes any failing stage fail the pipeline.

items.learning_item: Use Git branches, commits, pull requests, and merge-conflict resolution.

mcq.stem: You rebased your feature branch onto `main` and force-pushed. A teammate who had already pulled the branch now sees duplicated commits after running `git pull`. What happened?
options: The force-push failed partially, leaving both versions on the remote
Their Git version is older and cannot read rewritten history correctly
Duplicated commits are cosmetic; `git gc` removes them
The rebase duplicated the commits on your side, so you should have used `git merge` instead
The rebase gave your commits new SHAs, so their `pull` merged the old originals back in as well

distractor_rationale.misconception: The duplication is on their side, produced by the pull.
Force-push is atomic per ref.
Not a version issue.
The duplicates are real commits, not garbage.

mcq.explanation: Rebasing creates new commit objects. Their local branch still holds the originals, and a default `pull` merges the rewritten remote into that, so both copies of every commit survive. They recover with `git fetch && git reset --hard origin/<branch>` after saving any local work — which is why force-pushing a shared branch needs an explicit heads-up.

items.learning_item: Use Git branches, commits, pull requests, and merge-conflict resolution.

mcq.stem: After `git reset --hard HEAD~3` on a local branch, you realise two of those commits were never pushed anywhere. What is the accurate assessment?
options: The commits are permanently gone; only pushed commits can be recovered
They are unreachable but not deleted; `git reflog` still holds the previous HEAD
`git fsck --lost-found` is the only recovery path, because reset removes the reflog entries too
They can be recovered only if `git stash` was used before the reset
`git reset --hard` moves the branch pointer without touching the working tree, so the files are still on disk

distractor_rationale.misconception: Confuses unreachable with deleted.
`fsck` works as a fallback, but reset does not clear the reflog — which is the easier path.
Stash is unrelated to commit recovery.
Straightforwardly false: `--hard` is precisely the flag that overwrites the working tree.

mcq.explanation: `--hard` moves the branch pointer and overwrites the working tree, but the commit objects survive in the object database and the reflog records where HEAD pointed before the move. `git reflog` gives you the SHA and `git reset --hard <sha>` restores it. The window is real but not indefinite — unreachable objects are pruned by `git gc` after the expiry period, so recover promptly.

items.learning_item: Manage dependencies using virtual environments and dependency files.

code.title: Requirements file normaliser
code.prompt:
A dependency audit needs a canonical view of what a `requirements.txt` actually pins.

Implement `parse_requirements(lines)` returning a dict mapping normalised package name to its version specifier.

Processing rules per line:
1. Drop an inline comment: everything from the first occurrence of `" #"` (space followed by hash) onward.
2. Strip surrounding whitespace. Skip the line if it is now empty, starts with `#`, or starts with `-` (pip options such as `-r` or `-e`).
3. The package name is the leading run of letters, digits, `.`, `_` and `-`. Normalise it per PEP 503: replace every run of `-`, `_` or `.` with a single `-`, then lower-case.
4. An optional extras group in square brackets immediately after the name is discarded.
5. The specifier is everything remaining, with **all whitespace removed**. Use `""` when nothing remains.
6. If a normalised name appears more than once, the last occurrence wins.

examples.explanation: The comment line is skipped and `requests` has no specifier.
The `-r` include is an option line and is skipped.

tests.targets: Empty input.
Extras group discarded without corrupting the specifier.
PEP 503 normalisation makes these the same package; the last one wins.
Inline comment stripped and internal whitespace removed from the specifier.
Whitespace-only and full-line comments both skipped.
A compound specifier is preserved intact — do not split on the comma.

source_rubric_criteria.criterion: All tests pass, including extras, compound specifiers and duplicate normalisation.
Implements PEP 503 collapsing of `-`, `_` and `.` runs before lower-casing.
Correctly skips option lines, comments and blanks without special-casing each prefix ad hoc.
Parsing steps map recognisably onto the stated rules.

items.learning_item: Work with Linux commands, environment variables, and basic shell scripts.

code.title: Layered environment resolution with type coercion
code.prompt:
Configuration arrives from four sources with increasing precedence: packaged `defaults`, then `dotenv`, then `os_env`, then `cli`.

Implement `resolve_env(defaults, dotenv, os_env, cli)`. Start from `defaults` and apply the three override layers in order. Every override value is a string and must be coerced to the type of the **default** for that key:
- bool: `"1"`, `"true"`, `"yes"`, `"on"` (case-insensitive, surrounding whitespace ignored) become `True`; `"0"`, `"false"`, `"no"`, `"off"` and the empty string become `False`; anything else keeps the value currently held.
- int / float: parse it; on failure keep the value currently held.
- otherwise: use the string as-is.

Keys not present in `defaults` are ignored entirely — an unknown key never enters the result.
constraints: Each override layer has at most 500 keys
Default values are bool, int, float or str

examples.explanation: The string `"true"` is coerced to a boolean because the default is boolean.
`os_env` outranks `dotenv`, and `"False"` coerces to `False` rather than being truthy.

def resolve_env(defaults: dict, dotenv: dict, os_env: dict, cli: dict) -> dict:

Unparseable int falls back rather than raising or storing the string.
Scientific notation must parse as a float.
Unknown keys never enter the result.
Empty string is an explicit false, not a missing value.
Full precedence chain applied in order.
Unrecognised boolean token keeps the current value; `bool` must be checked before `int` since `bool` subclasses `int`.

source_rubric_criteria.criterion: All tests pass, including the bool-before-int ordering and fallback behaviour.
Layers applied in the specified order with no key leaking from an unknown source.
Boolean tokens handled explicitly rather than by Python truthiness of the string.
Coercion factored into a helper rather than inlined four times.

code.title: Impacted test selection
code.prompt:
To keep CI fast you only want to run tests for modules affected by a change.

`dependents` maps a module to the list of modules that **import it**. Given the modules changed in a pull request, implement `tests_to_run(changed, dependents)` returning every module transitively affected — including the changed modules themselves — sorted ascending with no duplicates.

The dependency graph may contain cycles.
constraints: Cycles are possible and must not cause infinite recursion

examples.explanation: `utils` affects `train` and `serve`, and `train` in turn affects `cli`.
Edges point from a module to its importers; `a` importing nothing from `b` means `a` is unaffected.

code.starter_code:
def tests_to_run(changed: list[str], dependents: dict[str, list[str]]) -> list[str]:
    ...

tests.targets: No changed modules means no tests.
A module absent from the graph still returns itself.
A cycle must terminate rather than recurse forever.
Duplicate input entries deduplicated.
Multiple roots converging on one dependent; output sorted, not in traversal order.
Deep transitive chain.

source_rubric_criteria.criterion: All tests pass, including cycles and missing graph entries.
Visited set consulted before expanding, so cycles terminate.
Traverses importers, not imports — does not reverse the graph.
Output sorted and deduplicated.

items.learning_item: Use Git branches, commits, pull requests, and merge-conflict resolution.

code.title: Line-based three-way merge
code.prompt:
Implement the core of a simplified merge driver: `three_way_merge(base, ours, theirs)`, where each argument is a list of lines.

Apply these rules in order:
1. If `ours == theirs`, return that content.
2. If `ours == base`, return `theirs`.
3. If `theirs == base`, return `ours`.
4. Otherwise let `p` be the length of the longest prefix on which all three lists agree line-for-line, and `s` the length of the longest suffix on which all three agree, where `p + s` may not exceed the length of the shortest list. Define each list's *middle* as the slice between its prefix and suffix. Then:
   - if `ours_mid == base_mid`, the merged middle is `theirs_mid`;
   - else if `theirs_mid == base_mid`, the merged middle is `ours_mid`;
   - else the merged middle is `["<<<<<<< ours"] + ours_mid + ["======="] + theirs_mid + [">>>>>>> theirs"]`.

Return prefix + merged middle + suffix.
constraints: Prefix and suffix must not overlap: p + s <= min(len(base), len(ours), len(theirs))

examples.explanation: `theirs` matches `base`, so our change is taken by rule 3.
Both sides changed the same middle line, so the region is marked as a conflict.

code.starter_code:
def three_way_merge(base: list[str], ours: list[str], theirs: list[str]) -> list[str]:
    ...

tests.targets: All three empty; rule 1 short-circuits.
Identical changes on both sides are not a conflict.
Pure append on our side only.
Conflicting appends with an empty base middle and a zero-length suffix.
Rule 2 fires before any prefix/suffix computation.
Non-adjacent edits still conflict under a single-region algorithm — the documented limitation, not a bug.
An empty `ours_mid` from a deletion must still emit conflict markers rather than being treated as unchanged.

source_rubric_criteria.criterion: All tests pass, including empty middles and the zero-suffix slicing case.
Handles `suffix_len == 0` without accidentally slicing away the whole list.
Applies the three short-circuit rules before computing prefix and suffix.
Middle extraction factored out rather than repeated three times.

items.learning_item: Use Git branches, commits, pull requests, and merge-conflict resolution.

voice.prompt:
Describe the branching and pull-request workflow you would set up for a four-person AI team shipping weekly.

Be concrete about what belongs in a pull request, what blocks a merge, and what you would deliberately leave unenforced.
follow_up_probes: A model file is 400 MB. How does that change the workflow?
What do you do when a PR has been open for five days?
Which of your rules would you drop first if the team said it was slowing them down?
expected_answer_outline: Picks a branching model and justifies it by team size and release cadence rather than by name-dropping GitFlow.
Defines PR contents: focused scope, description of intent, how it was verified, and what reviewers should look at.
Names blocking checks that are objective and fast — tests, lint, type check — and separates them from advisory ones.
Handles large artifacts explicitly: models and datasets do not belong in Git; LFS, object storage or a registry with a pointer in the repo.
Has a view on PR size and staleness, with a rule for splitting or closing.
Names something intentionally unenforced and explains the trade — e.g. commit message format, coverage percentage.
voice.sample_strong_answer:
For four people shipping weekly I would keep it simple: short-lived branches off `main`, one PR each, merged with squash. Anything heavier than that is ceremony for a team this size — GitFlow's release branches solve a problem we do not have.

A PR should be one intent. The description says what changed and why, and — the part most people skip — how it was verified. For an AI repo that means naming the dataset slice or the eval it was checked against, not just 'tested locally'. If a PR touches more than one concern I ask for a split, because review quality falls off a cliff past a few hundred lines.

Blocking: tests pass, lint passes, type check passes, one approval. Those are objective and fast, so nobody argues with them. Advisory: coverage numbers, architectural comments, style preferences. I keep those out of the blocking set on purpose, because a check that blocks and is subjective becomes a place where reviewers exercise personal taste and PRs sit for days.

Large artifacts are their own rule: model weights and datasets never go in Git. They go to object storage or a model registry, and the repo holds a pointer plus a hash. Once a 400 MB blob is in history, every clone pays for it forever.

On staleness, five days open means something is wrong — either the PR is too big or the reviewer is overloaded. My rule is that a stale PR gets split or closed, not nagged.

The first thing I would drop under pressure is commit message formatting. It has real value in a long-lived repo, but for four people who talk daily it is the lowest-yield rule I would be enforcing.

evaluation_criteria.criterion: Chooses a workflow proportionate to a four-person weekly-shipping team.
Specifies verification evidence, not just a description.
Separates objective blocking checks from advisory feedback with a reason.
Keeps large model/data artifacts out of Git history.

common_pitfalls: Naming GitFlow or trunk-based development without connecting it to team size or cadence.
No position on PR size or staleness.
Treating every possible check as blocking.
No mention of how model weights or datasets are versioned.
red_flags: Committing model checkpoints directly to the repository as normal practice.
Cannot name anything that would block a merge.

items.learning_item: Use Git branches, commits, pull requests, and merge-conflict resolution.

voice.prompt:
You rebased a shared branch and force-pushed. Two teammates pulled afterwards and now have duplicated commits, and one of them has lost a day of local work.

Walk me through the recovery, and then tell me what you would change so it does not happen again.
follow_up_probes: Their work is not in any commit — it is uncommitted in the working tree. Does that change anything?
What exactly does `--force-with-lease` protect against, and what does it not protect against?
Would you have made the same call on a personal branch?
expected_answer_outline: Stabilises first: tell everyone to stop pushing and pulling until the branch state is agreed.
Recovers the lost work through the reflog — `git reflog` finds the pre-pull HEAD, then a rescue branch or cherry-pick.
Distinguishes committed work (recoverable via reflog/fsck) from uncommitted work (not recoverable through Git at all, though editor history or `git stash` may help).
Cleans up the duplicated commits with `git fetch` plus a hard reset to the remote after preserving anything unique.

Explains `--force-with-lease`: it refuses the push if the remote moved since your last fetch, protecting against overwriting someone else's push — but not against rewriting history others already pulled.
Proposes durable prevention: protected branches with force-push disabled, rebase only on unshared branches, merge or squash-merge into shared ones, and communication before any history rewrite.
voice.sample_strong_answer:
First thing is to stop the bleeding — I would tell both teammates not to push or pull again until we agree on a state, because each additional pull creates more duplicate history to untangle.

Then recovery, and it depends on what 'lost work' means. If their commits exist locally, nothing is actually gone: `git reflog` shows where their HEAD was before the pull, and I can create a rescue branch at that SHA and cherry-pick anything unique onto the rewritten branch. If the work was uncommitted in the working tree and a pull or reset clobbered it, Git never saw it and cannot help — at that point it is editor local history or nothing. That distinction is the whole lesson, and it is worth saying out loud to the team.

For the duplicates, once anything unique is preserved, the clean move is `git fetch` and then reset hard to the remote branch, so everyone's local matches the rewritten history exactly.

On `--force-with-lease`: it checks that the remote ref is still where you last saw it, so it stops you from clobbering a colleague's push that landed after your fetch. What it does not do is protect people who have already pulled the old history — from their side the rewrite is just as disruptive. So it is a guardrail against one specific race, not a licence to rewrite shared branches.

Prevention is mostly policy, not tooling. Force-push disabled on protected branches. Rebase is for branches only I have touched; anything shared gets merged or squash-merged. And if a shared branch genuinely has to be rewritten, it is announced first and everyone re-clones or resets deliberately rather than discovering it through a confusing pull. I would not have made this call on my own branch — there it is fine, and that is exactly the line.

evaluation_criteria.criterion: Uses reflog correctly and preserves unique work before resetting.
Distinguishes what Git can and cannot recover.
Accurately states what the flag does and does not protect against.
Proposes policy-level prevention, not just 'be more careful'.

common_pitfalls: Claiming the commits are permanently lost.
Presenting `--force-with-lease` as making force-pushing safe in general.
Jumping to re-clone everything without preserving unique local commits.
Blaming the teammates for pulling.
red_flags: Suggests everyone delete and re-clone before checking whether unique work exists locally.
No understanding that rewriting shared history is the root cause.

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Uses reflog correctly and preserves unique work before resetting.
Distinguishes what Git can and cannot recover.
Accurately states what the flag does and does not protect against.
Proposes policy-level prevention, not just 'be more careful'.

items.learning_item: Manage dependencies using virtual environments and dependency files.

voice.prompt:
An ML repository trains on GPU and serves on CPU. Build me the reproducibility argument: `requirements.txt`, lock files, conda and Docker each solve part of the problem.

What does each actually guarantee, where does each fail, and what would you put in place for this repo?
follow_up_probes: Someone says 'the Docker image is the lock file'. Is that enough?
What is still not reproducible even with all of this in place?
How do you handle the CUDA build on GPU and the CPU wheel on the serving side?
expected_answer_outline: `requirements.txt` with direct pins captures intent but leaves transitive dependencies floating; a lock file with a fully resolved, hash-pinned set is what makes an install repeatable.
Lock files still do not pin the Python interpreter, system libraries, compilers or CUDA runtime — that is the layer Docker or conda covers.

conda handles non-Python binary dependencies (CUDA toolkit, MKL, BLAS) that pip historically could not; Docker pins the whole userspace but is only reproducible if the base image and the install steps are themselves pinned.
Notes that `FROM python:3.11` and unpinned `apt-get install` make a Dockerfile non-reproducible despite the image feeling frozen — digest pinning is required.
Handles the GPU/CPU split explicitly: separate environment files or extras, different torch build indices, one shared application code path.
Names what remains irreproducible: GPU non-determinism and kernel selection, data drift, model artifacts, and randomness that seeding does not fully control.
voice.sample_strong_answer:
I would layer it. `requirements.txt` with direct pins states what the project asks for — that is intent, and it is the file a human edits. It does not make anything reproducible on its own, because everything underneath is unpinned and a transitive release can change your environment overnight. The lock file is what actually fixes the install: a fully resolved set with hashes, generated by a tool, never edited by hand.

But a lock file only covers Python packages. It says nothing about the interpreter patch version, glibc, the compiler, or the CUDA runtime. That is the layer Docker covers, and conda partially covers by shipping binary non-Python dependencies. The subtlety with Docker is that people treat the image as automatically reproducible when the Dockerfile usually is not — `FROM python:3.11` follows a moving tag and `apt-get install` grabs whatever is current. If I want reproducibility I pin the base image by digest and pin apt packages, otherwise I have a frozen artifact built from an unfrozen recipe. The image is reproducible; the build is not, and those are different claims.

For this repo specifically I would split the environments rather than force one. Shared application code, two dependency sets — the training set installs the CUDA build of torch from the appropriate index, the serving set installs the CPU wheel — with a shared core requirements file so the versions of everything else cannot drift apart. Two Dockerfiles or one with build args. What I would not do is install the CUDA build in the serving image and rely on it falling back, because that is gigabytes of image for nothing.

And I would be honest about what none of this fixes. GPU kernel selection and reduction order are not deterministic by default, so bit-identical training runs need explicit deterministic flags and a performance cost. Data is not in any of these files — the dataset version has to be pinned separately. And the model artifact itself needs hashing and versioning, because in practice 'reproducible' usually means 'I can rebuild the same service around the same weights', not 'I can retrain and get identical weights'.

evaluation_criteria.criterion: Correctly separates what each tool guarantees and where its coverage stops.
Recognises that an unpinned base image or apt step makes a Dockerfile non-reproducible.
Proposes a workable split for the two runtimes without duplicating application code.
Names what stays irreproducible — GPU non-determinism, data, artifacts.

common_pitfalls: Treating Docker as a complete answer with no attention to how the image is built.
Conflating `pip freeze` output with a lock file.
No mention of the dataset or model artifact as versioned inputs.
Proposing one environment for both GPU training and CPU serving with no discussion of image size or wheel selection.
red_flags: Believes pinning Python dependencies alone makes training reproducible.
Unaware that GPU computation can be non-deterministic even with a fixed seed.
